# librechat_access_role (Data Source)

Reads one of LibreChat's ACL permission templates out of the `accessroles` collection - `agent_viewer`, `mcpServer_owner` and so on.

`librechat_grant` resolves these itself, so this data source is not needed to make a grant. It is here for the times the question is "what does `editor` actually allow": `perm_bits` is the bitmask LibreChat's permission checks compare against, and reading it is faster and more reliable than reasoning about which bits a release assigns.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# librechat_grant resolves these itself, so this is not needed to make a grant. It is for
# answering "what does editor actually allow": perm_bits is the bitmask LibreChat's permission
# checks compare against, and reading it beats reasoning about which bits a release assigns.
data "librechat_access_role" "agent_editor" {
  resource_type = "agent"
  name          = "editor"
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) Short role name - `viewer`, `editor`, `owner`. Combined with `resource_type` into the stored `accessRoleId`.
- `resource_type` (String) One of `agent`, `project`, `file`, `promptGroup`, `mcpServer`, `remoteAgent`, `skill`, `sharedLink`.

### Read-Only

- `access_role_id` (String) The composed identifier actually stored, e.g. `agent_viewer`.
- `description` (String)
- `display_name` (String) The name LibreChat shows in the sharing dialog.
- `id` (String) ObjectId of the accessroles document.
- `perm_bits` (Number) The permission bitmask. At the time of writing VIEW = 1, EDIT = 2, DELETE = 4, SHARE = 8, which makes `viewer` 1, `editor` 3 and `owner` 15 - but read the value rather than assuming it, which is the point of this data source.
